There is currently no cure for Alzheimer's disease, but multiple treatment categories exist [d1][d3][d6]. Established symptomatic medications include acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitors — donepezil, galantamine, and rivastigmine — for early-to-mid-stage disease, and memantine for moderate-to-severe cases; these work by modulating neurotransmitter levels but do not halt disease progression [d1][d5][d7]. More recently, the FDA has approved two disease-modifying monoclonal antibody therapies — lecanemab (Leqembi) and donanemab (Kisunla) — for people with mild Alzheimer's or mild cognitive impairment; clinical trials showed they slowed cognitive and functional decline by targeting and removing beta-amyloid plaques from the brain [d4][d6][d8]. Additional medications such as antidepressants and antipsychotics may be prescribed to manage behavioral symptoms like depression, agitation, and hallucinations [d2][d5]. Non-pharmacological approaches — including physical exercise, social activity, proper nutrition, and environmental adaptations (e.g., structured routines, safety modifications at home) — are also considered important components of a comprehensive care plan [d2][d6]. Investigational agents such as buntanetap, which targets amyloid protein, are also being studied in clinical trials [d9].
